text.tspan: The Heap is the ONE region shared by all threads — every thread's Stack is private to that thread.
Metaspace, Code Cache and Native memory are NOT part of the Heap and are NOT scanned by the object Garbage Collector
the same way heap objects are (Metaspace has its own GC-driven unloading tied to ClassLoader lifecycle).

It is a special, JVM-managed hash-table-
like region that stores String LITERALS
and INTERNED Strings only — never every
Prior to Java 7, the String Pool lived in PermGen (a fixed-size native memory region), which made it a common
source of OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space when applications interned too many Strings.
Since Java 7 (and PermGen's full removal in Java 8, replaced by Metaspace) the Pool lives in the Heap and is
scanned/collected by the ordinary object Garbage Collector, so unreferenced pooled Strings CAN be reclaimed.
Implementation detail: internally the pool is a native hash table (the JVM's StringTable, tunable with
-XX:StringTableSize). It starts EMPTY at JVM boot and is filled lazily as literals are first executed / classes are loaded,
and explicitly via String.intern(). It never stores ordinary heap Strings created only through concatenation or I/O.

svg.text: Old "Hello" object is never mutated — s is simply RE-POINTED to a new object.

text.tspan: The char array (or byte[] + coder, since JDK 9's Compact Strings) backing a String is `final` and never modified
after construction. Every "mutating" method (concat, substring, replace, toUpperCase...) returns a BRAND-NEW
String; the receiver object itself never changes. This guarantees String Pool safety (two refs can safely share
one object), thread-safety without locks, and safe use as HashMap keys (hashCode is cached once).

svg.text: GARBAGE COLLECTION OF THE OLD OBJECT

text.tspan: The old "Hello" object becomes eligible for GC only once NOTHING references it. If it is only a plain heap object
with no other refs, it can be collected. If it is the interned literal in the pool, it stays reachable (and alive) as
long as its defining ClassLoader is alive — pooled literals are not automatically freed just because a local var moved on.

svg.text: Same StringBuilder object, same memory address.
SAME reference, SAME object — internal char array expands in place.

text.tspan: StringBuilder mutates its internal char[]/byte[] buffer directly and resizes it as needed. Its methods are NOT synchronized — fastest choice for single-threaded string building (e.g. loops, `+` compiled by javac in many cases).

svg.text: Same StringBuffer object, same memory address.
SAME reference, SAME object — internal char array expands in place.

text.tspan: Same mutable buffer strategy as StringBuilder, but nearly every public method is `synchronized`, making it safe to share across multiple threads at the cost of lock-acquisition overhead. Prefer StringBuilder unless you truly share one instance.

Reference vs Object vs Memory location
A REFERENCE is a small value (like a typed pointer) held
in a variable. The OBJECT is the actual data structure
living at some MEMORY LOCATION on the Heap. Copying a
variable copies the reference, never the object.
Assignment (s2 = s1) copies the reference bits, so both
